title: Up a piece: trade, march, promote

difficulty.label: On-ramp conversion: the extra piece becomes an extra queen

objective.summary: You are a clean knight up and the opponent has offered you the one thing a winning side should always accept: a piece trade. The winning method is a sentence: trade pieces (never pawns), walk your king to the centre, use the knight to win pawns, push a passer, promote, mate with the new queen. This drill is graded on the result — finish the game.

assessedBy.note: Fifteen units are on the board, far beyond Syzygy's seven-piece ceiling, so the root assessment — a clean extra knight with level pawns is winning — is authored, not proved. It is concretely checkable with a fixed-depth engine pass, which has not been run.

planClasses.label: Trade pieces, keep pawns
planClasses.description: The winning side's exchange policy in one line: every PIECE trade shrinks their ability to resist while your extra knight stays extra; every PAWN trade shrinks the material your knight will eventually be exchanged into. The rook trade on d8 is this policy's first test.

planClasses.label: March the king
planClasses.description: With the rooks off there is no piece left that can punish a walking king — so the king stops being a liability and becomes your second extra piece. The model line spends three straight moves on the march and loses nothing by it.

planClasses.label: Raid with the knight
planClasses.description: The knight attacks what pawns cannot easily defend — b7, a7, the queenside targets. A legitimate accelerant AFTER the trade; as a substitute for trading it leaves the rooks on and the win slower and looser.

annotations: Accept. The rooks are each other's mirror — while both stand, their rook makes threats yours must answer; when both are gone, your knight is the only piece on the board. A piece trade when you are a piece up is never a concession: it is the win compressing.

The recapture is forced, and stop to see what you bought: the board now holds kings, pawns, and your knight. Every remaining move of this game is about one question — how does the extra piece become an extra queen?

The march begins. There is no rook left to check your king from behind, so the fastest path to the win runs THROUGH the middle of the board. At this band the winning side usually pushes pawns here; the model line spends its moves on the king first and the pawns keep their options.
They march too — the defender's best hope is an active king. Match them step for step and the extra knight decides every square the kings argue about.

Second step. Notice what you are NOT doing: not pushing pawns (nothing to fix yet), not raiding with the knight (it guards the queenside from c3 while the king travels). Quiet moves are easy when you are a piece up — that is what being a piece up is for.

Their king heads for the centre squares your king wants. This is the defender doing everything right — and it changes nothing about the count: on every contested square you will eventually stand king plus knight against king.

The armies are as close as they will ever be to equal-looking — two centralised kings, level pawns — and the game is still simply won, because from here the knight picks a flank, wins a pawn the king cannot defend in time, and escorts the passer. Play on and finish: the drill ends at checkmate, not at advantage.

checkpoints.label: Rooks off — choose your winning scheme
The march is done — the knight decides
End of the authored technique — the finish is yours

deviations.note: Ask the second question about your OWN move: what did the king stop doing on e1? Sharing the defence of d1. Nothing hangs — after 1...Rxd1+ the knight recaptures — but look where that leaves it: your winning piece dragged backward to d1, undeveloped by a king sidestep, and the trade happened on their initiative anyway. A free choice deferred is a small piece of the win given away.

The knight leaps to the beautiful central square — and the e6 pawn simply takes it. Count the cheapest attacker of the square you are moving to, every time, even when you are winning. Especially when you are winning: the whole advantage rides on this one piece.

The raid, one move early: Nb5 eyes a7 and c7 and still guards d-file entries badly. Black answers ...Rxd1+ Kxd1 and the trade happens anyway — on their initiative. Same destination, minus the tempo; the spine takes the trade first because free choices should be exercised, not deferred.

Not losing — planless. The pawn advances toward nothing while the rook trade stays pending on Black's terms. When you are winning, the first habit to drill is doing the forcing housekeeping (trades, threats answered) before any move that merely looks forward.

The same square, the same pawn, one move later — ...exd5 and the extra piece is gone, leaving a drawn-at-best pawn ending. Worth meeting twice on purpose: the blunder that costs the win rarely looks like a blunder, it looks like centralisation.

Now the raid is fully sound: rooks are off, Nb5 hits a7, and ...a6 is met by Nd4 with the queenside pawns fixed as targets. A faster, sharper road than the king march — the spine prefers the march because it is the same technique in every winning endgame, not just this one.

Pawns before the king. It cannot be punished here — nothing can punish you — but drills build defaults, and the default this position teaches is king first: the pawn that advances early fixes itself on squares the defender's king will attack later.
Starting the pawns while the king is half-marched. Same lesson, sharper form: every pawn move is one your king did not make, and pawns cannot move backward to undo what the advance loosened.

Third offer of the same square, cruellest version: now BOTH the e6 pawn and the king on d6 attack d5, and the knight is defended by nobody. When a square has been poisoned once, re-read it every single time — the poison does not expire because your position improved.

feedbackClaims.text: A piece up, every piece trade is a raise and every pawn trade is a pay cut: pieces off the board shrink their capacity to resist while your extra knight stays extra; pawns off the board shrink the queening material your knight exists to escort. Accept piece trades, decline pawn trades, and the endgame plays itself.

Once the last major piece leaves the board, the king's danger premium expires — there is nothing left to check it from a distance. From that move on, a king in the centre is worth roughly a minor piece of activity, and the side that marches first banks the difference.

This is an outcome drill resolved at the end of the game: you are graded on finishing the win, not on matching the model moves. A win by knight raid, by pawn storm, or by slow squeeze is a pass; the model line is one clean road, not the road.

The guard here is the material guard-rail (200 centipawns, about two-thirds of the knight): its teaching cases are the three Nd5 offers, each of which hands back the whole advantage in one move. Below that line it stays silent — a winning position played slowly is not an error at this band.

sources: Start position is a constructed schematic (White Ke1/Rd1/Nc3, pawns a2 b2 e3 f2 g2 h2; Black Ke8/Rd8, pawns a7 b7 e6 f7 g7 h7): a clean extra knight, symmetric pawns, rooks in mutual offer on the open d-file, both rooks defended by their kings so the trade is a choice, not a tactic. It is not taken from a game and no named theoretical position is claimed for it.

MECHANICAL: every spine move and every deviation move was replayed legal with chessops this session; `make pack-check` independently re-walks spine and deviation lint. The three Nd5 refutations (exd5 twice; exd5/Kxd5 at the third offer) are capture-legality facts on the derived positions. The Kf1 note's claim that nothing hangs was machine-checked the hard way: an earlier draft of this file classified 1.Kf1 as a rook-losing tactical_error, and the scratch harness refuted it — Nc3 recaptures on d1. The correction (trade still available, knight dragged to d1) is what the replay actually shows.

MECHANICAL: the degraded trigger is pawn-unit arithmetic (material_balance, white perspective, atMost 1) — it fires exactly when the extra piece has been given back, and cannot fire on the rook trade itself (the balance stays +3 through Rxd8+ Kxd8).

NO ENGINE ANALYSIS WAS RUN. Not one position in this pack has been seen by Stockfish at any depth. NO TABLEBASE GROUND TRUTH EXISTS for any node: fifteen units at the root, eleven after maximal spine trades — Syzygy stops at seven.

UNGROUNDED: the root assessment ('a clean knight up with level pawns is winning'), every plan-class description, every annotation, every deviation classification and note, and every feedbackClaim are agent-authored model knowledge with no citation, no engine validation and no reviewer sign-off.
graduationBlockers: There is no pack review workflow in this system and there never will be one (owner ruling 2026-08-13). Only a citable source or mechanical validation that bears on a claim clears a blocker.

The root authored assessment (win) is the pack's load-bearing claim. It is engine-checkable at fixed depth and — after enough trades — partially checkable against Syzygy on sub-lines; neither instrument has been run.
The claim that the pawn ending after any Nd5/exd5 give-back is 'drawn at best' is stated as a practical judgment and is engine-checkable; it has not been checked.

The win objective resolves at terminal play against human_common resistance, which means the learner must actually deliver mate — possibly forty-plus moves beyond the 8-ply authored horizon. Whether a 1000-1400 learner finishes rather than abandons is a play-test question the format cannot answer; if runs abandon, the fix is an authored mid-checkpoint resolution, which for a win objective the current grading vocabulary cannot express short of terminal.
The guard threshold (200cp) encodes the authored claim that give-backs are the only firing-worthy errors in a won position; no play-test evidence supports the number.
